newsitem.title: FRANCE: Carlos the Jackal demands ban on new book.
newsitem.headline: Carlos the Jackal demands ban on new book.

text.p: Jailed guerrilla mastermind "Carlos the Jackal" has demanded that a book about him published this week be banned on the grounds that it violates his right to be presumed innocent, justice sources said on Monday.

Venezuelan-born Carlos, in a Paris jail since his arrest in August 1994, has filed a suit prompted by "Carlos. The Secret Networks of International Terrorism", written by French journalist Bernard Violet and printed by Seuil publishing house.

The sources said Carlos had denounced the use of his picture on the front cover of the book. He demanded 350,000 francs ($70,000) as an advance payment in damages for what he termed an attack on his image and on his right to be presumed innocent.
Carlos, whose real name is Illich Ramirez Sanchez, formally objected to "the revelation of facts which pertain to his private life".

He demanded that distribution of the book be halted and that existing copies be seized. Failing that, he demanded a statement inside each copy of the book clarifying that "his participation in the events mentioned has never been established".
Asked to comment, a spokeswoman for Seuil would only say: "We are preparing to plead at the hearing (at the Paris lawcourts) on Tuesday.
"The photograph on the cover has already been published. It's not a picture we asked someone to take, obviously," she said. She refused to say how many copies of the book had been printed.
There was no immediate comment from Carlos's lawyer.

The book draws on questioning of Carlos by Paris anti-terrorism judge Jean-Louis Bruguiere, files of the former East Germany's Stasi secret services and other material to draw up a biography of the guerrilla.
Spirited to France after he was seized in Sudan, Carlos was sentenced to life in prison in his absence for shooting dead two French secret service agents in 1975.
Accused by the Interior Ministry of killing 83 people in a series of attacks mostly in Europe and the Middle East, he is under investigation for four other bombings in France in the 1980s.
Later in 1975 he led the kidnapping of 11 OPEC oil ministers from a conference in Vienna.
